c0958: Each tab's counter counts only the ✓; N/A items come out of the total.
c0669: Pick your legal model: dry hire by default (your client buys the alcohol; you bring the bar, the bartenders and everything else) or licensed full-service
c0672: Dry hire means the host buys and owns the alcohol and you sell service only. Full-service needs a licensed partner, your own license tied to a location, or a per-event permit. Your choice decides Phase 2; ask your state ABC before you advertise either one.
c0673: Hire an accountant or bookkeeper and set up quarterly estimated taxes
c0676: Ask for experience with event or service businesses. Estimated taxes are due quarterly; move a share of every deposit into a tax savings account so the bill never surprises you.
c0677: Choose your structure with your accountant: single-member LLC, sole proprietor or S corp
c0680: An LLC separates your personal assets from business liability, which matters when you work at weddings with alcohol on site. An S corp election can lower self-employment tax once profit is steady; ask your accountant when it pays off.
c0681: Register your LLC with the Secretary of State, appoint a registered agent and sign an operating agreement
c0684: File the articles of organization on your Secretary of State website. Fees and processing times vary by state. Sign an operating agreement even if you are the only member; venues and banks may ask for it.
c0685: Get your free EIN for the LLC from the IRS and register for state payroll and unemployment tax
c0688: Apply online at irs.gov once the LLC is filed; it is free and takes minutes. Then register with your state workforce agency before your first hire, so your payroll provider can file W-2 bartenders from day one.
c0689: Open a business bank account and keep your finances separate
c0692: Bring your EIN letter and formation documents. Use one card for purchases and a separate account for client deposits, so event deposits never mix with personal money.
c0693: Get your seller's permit (sales tax permit) and find out if bar service is taxable in your state
c0696: Apply with your state tax agency (California: cdtfa.ca.gov). In some states the whole invoice is taxable, including bartender service and rentals. Confirm the rule and whether service charges are taxed before you quote.
c0697: Apply for the city or county business license, plus a DBA if you use a trade name
c0700: Check every city where you plan to work: some require a license to operate there. A DBA (fictitious business name) is filed with the county or the state. Keep copies for venue paperwork.
c0701: Choose booking software and a CRM for proposals, e-signed contracts, deposits and balances
c0704: One tool should send the quote, collect the e-signature and take the deposit by card. Test it with a mock proposal before you pay for a full year.
c0705: Have an attorney draft your service agreement with dry-hire clauses
c0708: Cover: the host buys and owns the alcohol and keeps any leftovers; no cash bar, drink tickets, ticketed entry that includes drinks or donations; gratuity terms in writing where your state allows them; deposit and tiered cancellation; guest count changes; power access; photo use. Ask your attorney to check it against your state ABC rules.
c0709: Search and register your brand name with the USPTO and secure the domain
c0712: Run a free search on uspto.gov before you print a logo or a trailer wrap. Buy the .com and matching social handles the same day. A federal trademark application is optional at the start but worth considering for a name you will wrap on a trailer.
c0718: Look up your state's alcohol rules for a bartending-only service and save the answer in writing
c0721: Rules vary by state: Missouri ATC Circular 24-01 allows service-only work with no state license but warns about entry fees, tip jars and surcharges; Montana bans pre-stocked bars and allows private events only; check Texas (TABC), California, Florida and New York with your state ABC. Email the question and keep the reply.
c0722: Rent a storage unit or garage for your gear and trailer parking
c0725: Look for roughly 160-270 sq ft (15-25 m²) with drive-up access and room to hitch. Ask about 24-hour access, power for charging, insurance requirements and the deposit. Check your HOA or city rules on parking a trailer at home.
c0726: Ask your county health department if a permit applies to cut garnish and bagged ice
c0729: There is no mobile bar permit in most counties, so ask by phone or email whether mobile food vendor rules apply to you. Ask if cut garnish needs a licensed commercial kitchen (commissary), and whether a hand sink in the trailer is required. Use only commercial bagged ice.
c0730: Ask each event organizer who pulls the permit for public events
c0733: In dry hire the organizer usually holds the special event permit. If you ever serve alcohol under your own license, you may need a temporary or special event permit from your state ABC. Get the answer in writing.
c0734: Collect each venue's requirements: COI, additional insured, load-in hours, power, glass and ice rules, preferred vendor list
c0737: Ask your top 10 local venues for their vendor packet. Most want a certificate of insurance (COI) naming them as additional insured, load-in times and proof of alcohol server certification. Keep a one-page cheat sheet per venue.
c0738: Buy a used bar trailer: 6 x 12 ft (1.8 x 3.7 m) cargo, concession or horse trailer, with an inspection
c0741: Check frame, axles, tires, brakes, lights and roof leaks before you pay. Confirm your tow vehicle's rated towing capacity exceeds the loaded trailer weight, with some margin. Get the title and a bill of sale.
c0742: Title and register the trailer with your state DMV and add commercial auto coverage
c0745: Bring the title, bill of sale and ID to the DMV for registration and plates. Call your insurance agent: personal auto policies often exclude business use, so ask for commercial auto, or a commercial-use endorsement covering the trailer.
c0746: Convert the trailer: bar top, cabinets, hand sink, water tanks, LED lighting, wiring and wrap
c0749: Get at least two quotes from trailer builders or plan a careful DIY build. Fresh and gray water tanks, an ice bin and a hand sink are the usual must-haves. Book the wrap installer early; wrap lead times can run weeks.
c0750: Buy general liability insurance and request COIs with additional-insured wording
c0753: Ask an agent who insures event vendors. Most venues require a COI naming them as additional insured, often with $1 million per occurrence. Ask for the COI to be issued within 24 hours of a request.
c0754: Buy liquor liability insurance as a separate policy
c0757: General liability usually excludes alcohol. Liquor liability is separate, can start around $500-600 a year, and most venues and planners will not book you without it. Quote it with your general liability from one agent.
c0758: Buy workers' compensation for your W-2 bartenders and barbacks
c0761: Required in almost every state once you have employees. Your payroll provider can often bundle it and bill by payroll. Use accurate job classes for bartenders; misclassification shows up in audits.
c0762: Insure your gear in transit with inland marine (equipment floater) coverage
c0765: Ask for a policy that covers the portable bar, glassware and equipment while on the road and at venues. Keep an inventory with photos and purchase prices ready for the application.
c0766: Only if you go full-service: get your state's caterer's alcohol permit or a licensed partner; otherwise mark this "not applicable"
c0768: Only if you leave dry hire
c0769: Examples: Texas Caterer's Permit tied to a Mixed Beverage Permit, California Type 58 for on-sale licensees only, Florida 13CT, New York Caterer's Alcohol Permit per event. Ask your state ABC and an attorney first; in dry hire, mark it "not applicable".
c0772: Build or buy a portable bar for your second crew and indoor venues
c0775: A folding or modular portable bar lets you run two events on the same night and work ballrooms where the trailer cannot go. Check its width against standard doorways and elevator sizes before you buy.
c0776: Set up a commercial bagged-ice supplier and buy ice bins (60 lb (27 kg))
c0779: Plan about 1.5 lb (0.68 kg) of ice per guest as a Kit estimate. Size ice bins and coolers in quarts or lb, and get a standing account with a local ice company for event days. Always use commercial bagged ice.
c0780: Buy coolers for mixers and for the host's drinks
c0783: Size for the biggest event you plan to take. A 200 qt (about 190 L) cooler is the largest most people can move with two helpers. Keep host alcohol separate from your mixers and label it.
c0784: Choose glassware (about 300 pieces with racks) or quality disposable cups, depending on the venue
c0787: Some venues ban glass outdoors or near pools, so ask first. Buy racks that go straight to the glass washer. Price disposables per guest against the cost of washing and breakage.
c0788: Buy bar tools for 4 stations: shakers, jiggers, speed rails, strainers, bar spoons, bottle openers and dispensers
c0791: Standard jiggers hold 1 oz and 2 oz (30 and 59 ml). Buy one full set per station plus 20% spares. Label every kit with a number so it returns to the right crew.
c0792: Create props and a printed drink menu sign for your specialty bars: mimosa bar, espresso martini bar, tiki or speakeasy
c0795: Specialty bars are your differentiator and carry a surcharge. Make one reusable kit per theme: signs, garnish trays, serving glasses and a printed drink menu.
c0796: Install the inverter generator and load-test the trailer with everything on
c0799: Plug in lights, fridge, pumps and speaker for 30 minutes and watch the load. Many venues require a quiet generator or ask for a dedicated venue outlet, so get both options ready.
c0800: Sign a rate agreement with a party rental company for extra glassware, tables and linens
c0803: Ask for a trade account with a set discount and next-day return. Send a quote request for tables, linens and glassware racks so you can add them to your add-on prices.
c0804: Open accounts with suppliers for mixers, syrups and garnish at a restaurant supply store or club store
c0807: Compare unit prices per fl oz. Ask for a business account and a resale certificate where you resell supplies. Buy in bulk for syrups and juices that keep.
c0808: Stock disposables: cups, straws, napkins, coasters and menu signs
c0811: Buy for at least two events at a time. Keep a branded set for weddings and a plain one for corporate events. Order menu signs with the logo through a local print shop.
c0812: Label and inventory all your gear and create a trailer load-out checklist
c0815: Number every tool kit, cooler and crate. Keep a printed load-out list on the trailer door and photograph a fully packed trailer, so any bartender can check it.
c0816: Run a full dry run of an event: setup, service and breakdown, timed
c0819: Use friends as guests. Time the setup, make 50 drinks in 20 minutes and then break down. Fix whatever slows you down, then use the times in your quotes.
c0822: Create a staffing plan per event: 1 bartender per 50 guests for a full bar, 1 per 75 for beer and wine, plus a barback at large events
c0825: These ratios are a Kit estimate; adjust after your first events. Add one barback when the event has over 150 guests or two stations. Use the Pricing Calculator to cost each event.
c0826: Build a bench of W-2 event bartenders and barbacks (not 1099 contractors)
c0829: Hire as part-time W-2 employees; treating bartenders as independent contractors is a misclassification risk under the FLSA and California AB5. Recruit through bartending schools, local bars and Indeed.
c0830: Prepare offer letters, I-9 and W-4 for every hire and check your state minimum wage
c0833: Complete the I-9 within 3 business days of the start date and keep it on file. Check your state and city minimum wage and your tipped wage rules; they differ widely.
c0834: File new-hire reports with your state
c0837: Every state requires new-hire reporting, usually within 20 days. Your payroll provider can submit it for you.
c0838: Sign up with a payroll provider and link your workers' comp policy to payroll
c0841: Pick a payroll provider that handles tax filings, W-2s and workers' comp payments. Link your payroll to your bank account before the first event.
c0842: Check the minimum age to serve alcohol in your state and get a food handler card only if the state or county requires it for ice and garnish
c0845: Minimum serving ages and permit rules differ by state, and sometimes by county. Ask your state ABC and county health department. If a food handler card is required, get it for every crew member. Some cities and counties also require a bartender or server permit: ask them too.
c0846: Get all bartenders alcohol server certified: TABC in Texas, RBS in California, or TIPS / ServSafe Alcohol
c0849: Venues and insurers ask for it. Texas does not require it by law, but certified staff give the employer extra protection. Most courses take 2-4 hours online.
c0850: Train the crew on OSHA basics: glass cuts, lifting and towing safely
c0853: Cover safe lifting for ice and crates, broken glass cleanup, and trailer hitching and backing up. Keep a first-aid kit and a spill kit on the trailer.
c0854: Train on responsible service: check IDs, refuse minors and intoxicated guests, call last call and log incidents
c0857: Role-play three cases: an underage guest, an over-served guest and a host who wants you to keep pouring. Write a one-page incident log and keep it on the trailer.
c0858: Set your tip and service charge policy: tips go to staff (FLSA); a service charge is wages (IRS Rev. Rul. 2012-18)
c0861: A service charge is part of the invoice and is taxable income; a voluntary gratuity belongs to staff. Add a tip jar or a gratuity line only where your state does not treat it as a sale (Missouri may).
c0864: Create your brand, logo, signature cocktails menu and professional photos of the trailer set up
c0867: Shoot the trailer at golden hour and at a staged wedding table. Order 8-10 photos: trailer, signature cocktails, bartender in action and a specialty bar. These are your best sales tool.
c0868: Launch a website with packages, "from" prices per guest and a quote request form
c0871: Show 3 packages with a price per guest and an hourly rate for bartender-only service. Explain dry hire on the first screen and add the shopping list as a downloadable example.
c0872: Claim your Google Business Profile and start collecting reviews
c0875: Choose a service-area business listing, add photos of events and ask the first 5 clients for a review the day after the event. Reply to every review within 48 hours.
c0876: Create profiles on The Knot, WeddingWire and Zola
c0879: Upload your photos and the full package list. Weddings are your biggest revenue engine, so ask each profile for its lead response time and cost before you pay.
c0880: Join gig marketplaces: GigSalad (about 5% / 2.5% fee per confirmed booking), The Bash and Thumbtack (pay per lead)
c0883: Compare fees against your lead costs before paying. Only pay when you can reply within an hour, and set a minimum booking price so low-margin leads get filtered out.
c0884: Prospect event planners, office managers and HR teams for holiday parties and corporate events
c0887: Send 10 short emails a week with a one-page package and a photo. Start in September, since holiday parties book out by October.
c0888: Sign preferred-vendor deals with venues, wedding planners, photographers and DJs
c0891: Offer an introductory rate or a referral thank-you. Ask venues to put you on their preferred vendor list and send a thank-you gift after the first booking.
c0892: Set your tasting and drink menu consultation policy for couples and planners
c0895: Decide if tastings are free, paid or credited toward the booking. Bring three signature cocktails and a mocktail. Limit tastings to booked or serious leads.
c0896: Post on Instagram, Pinterest and reels with real events
c0899: Post 3-4 times a week at first. Short videos of the trailer setup and a cocktail being poured perform well. Tag the venue and the planner every time.
c0900: Set up a quote template with the Kit calculator and track every lead in your CRM
c0903: Use the calculator to get your cost per guest and price per guest; your minimum is an input there. Send each quote within 24 hours and follow up after 3 days.
c0904: Launch a referral program and ask for a review after every event
c0907: Offer a small thank-you for referrals once the new client books. Text or email the review request 48 hours after the event, with a direct link.
c0908: Join a local bridal show or hold a showcase for planners and venues; book your first 3 pilot events for the portfolio
c0911: Bridal shows book months out, so reserve early. Offer pilot events at a reduced rate in exchange for photos, a video and a written review.
c0914: Hold a client briefing 3 weeks before the event: guests, hours, package, specialty bar, venue and restrictions
c0917: Confirm guest count, hours, signature cocktails and any dietary or non-alcoholic needs. Send a written summary and the dry-hire reminder that the host buys the alcohol.
c0918: Do a site visit or walkthrough call 2 weeks out: trailer access, power, water and venue rules
c0921: Confirm load-in time, where you park, outlet location and amps, ice storage and the venue's rules on glass. Photograph the space for your crew.
c0922: Send the host the shopping list 2 weeks out and buy mixers, garnish and ice the day before
c0925: Use the Kit calculator for bottles by category, beer, wine and ice. The host buys and owns the alcohol; you buy mixers, garnish and ice. Keep receipts for your records.
c0926: Invoice the balance before the event and track deposits
c0929: Send the final invoice a week out. Mark deposits as paid and keep any service charge as a separate line; add a gratuity line only where your state does not treat it as a sale.
c0930: Run the trailer load-out checklist: hitch, lights and glass secured
c0933: Check hitch pin, safety chains, tire pressure and brake lights. Strap down crates and racks. Photograph the packed trailer.
c0934: Set up 60-120 minutes early, serve the event and call last call
c0937: Arrive on time, test the lights, power and water, then set the bar. Announce last call 15-30 minutes before closing, as agreed with the host.
c0938: Break down, count the glassware, hand leftover alcohol back to the host and return rentals
c0941: The host owns the leftover alcohol, so pack it as theirs and sign for the count. Clean the trailer, count glass and return rentals by the agreed return time.
c0942: Ask for a review and photos within 48 hours and follow up in the CRM
c0945: Send a short thank-you with a direct review link and ask the planner or venue for photos. Log the event outcome in your CRM.
c0946: Review monthly: cost per guest, staff hours and disposables against the calculator
c0949: Compare actual mixer, ice and cup costs per guest with your quotes. Check labor hours by event and fix any event that fell below your target margin.
c0950: Run a 90-day review: prices per guest, minimums, packages and specialty bars; continue training and visit industry events
c0953: Raise prices where you are always booked. Retire packages nobody buys. Consider events such as Bar Convent Brooklyn or Tales of the Cocktail and refresh your server certifications.
